name: Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers
title: Pattern 4: Hints, Not Answers
answer: Hints, Not Answers is the fourth of the book's ten patterns, and it means an AI tutor is set up to ask questions and offer clues instead of handing over the solution. It matters because the study the book opens with found that a tutor which gives answers makes practice easier while making learning worse, whereas a tutor that gives hints protects learning.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: The pattern grows directly out of the study that opened Chapter 1, where a tutor that gives answers made practice easier and learning worse, while a tutor that gives hints protected learning (Bastani et al., 2025). In practice it means that whatever the product is, it is configured to ask questions, offer clues, and require the student to attempt the work before it helps further. The problem it solves is that help arriving too quickly removes the struggle that produces learning, even though that help feels smoother and more satisfying in the moment. Because most general chat tools do not behave this way on their own, a school has to set them up deliberately rather than assume the default behaviour is safe. The pattern is simple to describe, but it depends on configuration and on adult presence rather than on the tool's own instincts.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the early grades the pattern mostly belongs to the teacher rather than the child, so a second grade teacher might use AI to plan a set of guiding questions for a reading group and then ask those questions out loud herself. In high school, students might use a configured tutor for homework, with the conversation log visible to the teacher. Setting this up is a matter of configuration, and with a school account in a tool such as Gemini for Education a teacher can write standing instructions telling the tool never to hand over a complete solution and to ask first what the student has already tried. The strongest results in the research came when adults set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room. In the Nigerian trial described in Chapter 1, teachers wrote the opening prompt for every session and walked the room the whole time (De Simone et al., 2025).
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book grounds this pattern in research rather than in opinion. It cites Bastani et al., 2025 for the finding that a tutor giving answers makes practice easier and learning worse while a tutor giving hints protects learning, and it cites De Simone et al., 2025 for the Nigerian trial in which teachers wrote the opening prompt for every session and walked the room the whole time. The book also reports that the strongest results in the research came when adults set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room. Figure 2.4 is described as showing the difference between the two kinds of tool at a glance. The text does not attach a separate evidence label to this pattern beyond these citations.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main limit is that general chat tools do not work this way on their own, so a school that does nothing ends up with a tool that will simply supply answers. Configuration is therefore a decision that stays with people, since a teacher writes the standing instructions that forbid a complete solution and require the tool to ask what the student has tried first. Adult presence is part of the pattern, because the strongest results came when adults set the tool up carefully and stayed in the room, and in the Nigerian trial teachers wrote the opening prompt for each session and walked the room throughout. In the early grades the pattern belongs to the teacher rather than the child, which keeps the questioning in human hands. In high school, where students may work with a configured tutor, the conversation log stays visible to the teacher so that oversight is not handed over to the tool.
